claims.support_note: Git's tutorial and the kubectl quick reference both show those tools used by typed commands; the sentence about what this module introduces is its own scope.
The supplied GUI article defines interaction through icons and visual indicators and direct manipulation of graphical elements such as windows and menus.
The same article says menus compile available commands and widgets present visual choices, which supports the qualified visual-work claims.
MDN calls the terminal a text interface, and Ubuntu says a typed command runs on Enter and prints its result.
Ubuntu says the prompt means the computer is ready, and the GUI article says modern systems provide both a GUI and a command-line interface.
Ubuntu treats commands as text that can be copied, saved, and run again, and the check-before-repeating clause is the page's instruction.
The GUI row matches visible direct manipulation, with the article's contrast that command lines require typed commands and become slow for long exact input.
Ubuntu describes a text command interface, the GUI article covers visual exploration, and the Windows Terminal announcement includes remote shell tabs such as SSH.
Ubuntu says command-line file operations are useful for repeated bulk changes, and the page keeps the GUI and pre-change check qualified.
Apple Bash documents a for-loop that repeats one action, and POSIX mv is the rename operation named by the example.
POSIX mv attempts to remove an existing destination, so the illustrated rename can overwrite, and the page says not to run it.
Spotlight's Command-Space and Return open a result, Apple's Terminal guide says to search for Terminal, and Ubuntu documents Ctrl-Alt-T plus a usual launcher.
Windows Terminal hosts PowerShell, Command Prompt, and WSL shells; WSL supplies Linux commands; PowerShell precedence shows aliases or functions can hide a name.
Microsoft's install page specifies administrator PowerShell, wsl --install, a restart, Ubuntu by default, and the already-installed caveat, and the page says not to run it.
Apple's example prompt ends in % and depends on settings, while Ubuntu's examples end in $, so user, host, and directory are not guaranteed.
Ubuntu and the Windows Terminal FAQ separate the window from the shell, and Apple says the window's prompt means a command can be entered.
Apple says the default shell is zsh and can be changed, Ubuntu's tutorial uses Bash, and PowerShell documents its own prompt and command language.
The Mac receipt shows Bash > and zsh dquote> with continuation variables unset, PSReadLine's default continuation is configurable >>, and PowerShell's built-in prompt can end in >.
Both isolated Mac shells treated a leading $ as the command and returned command not found.
Ubuntu shows the ready prompt after a finished command, and Apple Bash uses PS1 when ready and PS2 when more input is required.
Ubuntu says some commands print nothing and still return a prompt, and the Mac PTYs also showed command-not-found errors.
The named no-operand commands print text, the clock, the effective user, or the host name, while Bash aliases and PowerShell precedence can select a different command.
The Mac command printed Hello, World! without the quotes, and zsh history expansion applies inside double quotes but not single quotes.
whoami prints the effective user, and Ubuntu's superuser section shows that account identity can change what files can be modified.
Zsh, Bash, and PowerShell all allow the prompt text to be replaced, so the page's labeled two-tab scene treats labels as clues rather than proof.
Apple says the visible prompt depends on settings, and whoami plus hostname are the separate read-only checks the answer requires.
Ubuntu distinguishes the command, options that change it, and arguments that supply the data it acts on.
Apple Bash says the first word is the command and later words are its arguments, which fits the page's statement that its bracketed diagram means optional.
Bash defines an unquoted space as a word separator, and both PowerShell and Ubuntu show quotes grouping text that contains spaces.
Zsh removes quote characters after expansion, and the observed echo output did not contain the quoting characters.
GNU date 9.12 help documents -u as UTC, the Mac date -u output was marked UTC, and the date manual contrasts that with TZ or the system default.
The supplied GNU date usage is a command plus options and an optional format, so date -u needs no extra operand.
Ubuntu describes short and long option forms, and GNU date help includes -u, --utc, --help, and --version.
PSReadLine waits on an unclosed quote, Bash uses PS2 for incomplete input, and this Mac Bash build showed > .
Ubuntu shows an unquoted space creating two arguments, while quoted spaced text is passed as one argument.

The complete Apple termios manual's default is VINTR ^C, and INTR generates SIGINT for the controlling terminal's foreground process group when ISIG is enabled, with the character changeable or disableable; Mac Ctrl+C returned the prompt and PSReadLine can copy selected text instead.
These Mac builds showed > and dquote>, PSReadLine's documented default is configurable >>, and the page tells the reader to judge the incomplete command rather than one glyph.
PowerShell's subexpression operator inserts a statement such as Get-Date, and both whoami manuals report the current account.
Bash command substitution and the PowerShell subexpression run the inner statement before the outer command receives its text, and this lesson's example only prints.
PowerShell's built-in prompt already ends in >, Ubuntu separates a finished command from continued output, and Bash PS2 is the needs-more-input state.
The same default ^C-to-INTR-to-SIGINT rule covers the foreground process group when ISIG is set, the Mac sleep was interrupted, and CopyOrCancelLine copies when text is selected.
Ubuntu gives Ctrl-C as one cancellation and q as less's own quit key, while termios identifies SIGINT as the signal INTR sends, so the ignored-signal case stays a deferred boundary.
Zsh reports command not found after a failed search, the Mac PTYs showed that for a typo and a copied prompt, and Ubuntu shows wrong command case failing.
Apple Bash does not expand aliases in non-interactive shells unless enabled, and the quick reference includes the full kubectl get pods command.
Copying the lesson's leading $ made both Mac shells try to run $ and report command not found.
Bash aliases exist only where that shell defines them and are not expanded non-interactively unless expand_aliases is set.
Ubuntu's Ctrl-C cancellation and the Mac unfinished-quote cancellation return a prompt while leaving the session and its messages available.
IBM's history says characters were encoded as holes and each card was later inserted into a separate reader.
The VT100 guide sends keyboard input to the computer and displays returned data on the screen, matching Ubuntu's split between the window and the interpreting shell.

Terminal tabs can attach to different local or remote shells, while whoami and hostname are separate from the prompt label.

D1.quote: - **Compare** graphical interfaces and terminal interfaces, then choose the better tool for a beginner engineering task.
D1.why: Four outcomes use observable verbs through compare, diagnose, interpret, and debug, and each is taught and then tested.

D2.quote: This module compares a GUI with a terminal. You will open a terminal, read a prompt, try commands that print information, and practice recovering from an unfinished line.
D2.why: Each section builds from interface choice through commands and quoting into recovery, with worked examples before the exercise.

D3.quote: Pause and predict: if you had to rename hundreds of files the same way, which interface would you choose, and why?
D3.why: Prediction prompts, comparison checks, and reveal-after-answer questions occur through the body rather than only at the end.

D4.quote: For this introductory module, the decision framework is deliberately simple. Choose the terminal when the task is textual, repeatable, remote, scriptable, or easier to document as commands. Choose a GUI when the task is visual, one-off, exploratory, or better understood by direct manipulation. Choose both when the GUI helps you inspect the state and the terminal helps you perform or record the action precisely.
D4.why: The page ties commands to session identity, timestamps, and recovery consequences, with hypothetical scenes labeled and tradeoffs bounded.

D5.quote: Test your understanding by answering each scenario before opening the explanation, then compare your reasoning with the detailed answer.
D5.why: Eight scenario answers explain the display and the next move, and together they cover all four stated outcomes.

D6.quote: For this practice, change one thing between attempts. Changing the command name, quotes, and current directory together leaves several possible explanations for a different result. Make one correction, run once, and read the output before choosing the next correction.
D6.why: Sections, integrated tables, and one-change practice keep the load manageable, while the necessary shell branches still add weight.

D7.quote: That single symbol is easy to underestimate. It means the shell is ready for a command, much like a blank search box means a browser is ready for a query.
D7.why: The pace and examples stay precise, and the ready-state comparison is limited to that one mapping.

D8.quote: Try the pattern "predict, run, compare": before pressing Enter, state what you expect the command to do; afterward, compare the output with your prediction.
D8.why: For this medium tier the page supplies a pattern, an anti-pattern table, and a situation-to-tool guide before asking for independent diagnosis.

L1.quote: Diagnose frozen terminals. This final task is unguided: there are no commands to run and no steps to follow, only evidence to read. Each transcript below is a simulated snapshot of a terminal window frozen at one moment. For each transcript, write down two things in your notes before opening the answer key: what state the shell is in (ready, running, waiting for more input, or returned to the prompt after an error), and what your next move would be.
L1.why: Early tasks give the exact safe command, but the objective requires a predict-run-read loop and the final task removes the commands and asks for state plus a next move. That is guided scenario practice: more than copy-paste, and short of an immersive broken environment, so 4 rather than 3 or 5.

L2.quote: Open a terminal, run safe information commands, practice one recovery move, and finish by diagnosing frozen terminal snapshots without typing anything. This exercise is intentionally small because the goal is not speed. The goal is to build a reliable loop: predict the output, run the command, read the result, and confirm that the prompt returned.
L2.why: The tasks move from recognition and single commands through composition and cancellation to combined transcript diagnosis.

L3.quote: - [ ] Run the date/time command for your shell (`date` in Bash/zsh/WSL or `Get-Date` in PowerShell) and explain why your output differs from the example.
L3.why: Success requires explaining output, connecting identity commands to the session, and diagnosing state, alongside several run-and-see steps.

L4.quote: If you typed only `echo 'Hello, World!'`, the terminal should print `Hello, World!` and return to the prompt. If you copied `$ echo 'Hello, World!'` and received an error, remove the leading prompt symbol and run the command again. That correction is part of the learning objective, not a sign that you failed.
L4.why: The guidance names the likely copied-prompt mistake and the correction, and the other solution blocks explain what the display means.

L5.quote: Transcript A shows unfinished quoted input; finish the quote or cancel and compare with the normal prompt. Transcript B shows continuing output without a returned prompt; try Ctrl+C once and check the result. Transcript C shows a copied `$` prompt symbol being treated as a command; retype `echo 'Hello, World!'` without it. In the synthetic Transcript D, choose the window labeled `alex@training-vm /tmp $`. In real sessions, confirm the connection you opened and read the user/hostname checks before changing anything; customized labels alone are not proof.
L5.why: The lab ends by making the learner apply the same diagnosis, before opening the key, to four related frozen situations, including a different machine and a still-running command, and the key states that real labels are not proof. That is practiced transfer, so this is the lab dimension that reaches 5; a generalization sentence alone would have stayed at 4.

prior_finding_dispositions.quote: In Unix terminals, Ctrl+C normally generates an interrupt signal, SIGINT.
